core: U.S. neutrality 1914-1917 and why it eroded: economic ties to the Allies, German unrestricted submarine warfare, and the sinking of the Lusitania (7 May 1915)
The Zimmermann Telegram (January 1917) and its role in turning American opinion
The U.S. declaration of war (April 1917) and mobilization: the Selective Service Act and the draft, war-production agencies, and Liberty Bond financing

The home front: the Committee on Public Information and propaganda; the wartime crackdown on dissent via the Espionage Act (1917) and Sedition Act (1918); and the Great Migration of Black Americans to Northern cities
The American military contribution in 1918: the American Expeditionary Forces under Pershing, key 1918 battles, casualties, and the armistice of 11 November 1918
Wilson's Fourteen Points (8 January 1918) and the push for a League of Nations
The aftermath: the Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles and League membership, and the U.S. turn toward isolationism
supporting: Women entering wartime work and the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment (1920)
The 1919 Red Scare and Red Summer as part of the difficult postwar transition
Henry Cabot Lodge, the reservationists, and Article X of the League Covenant
outOfScope: The global course of World War I — causes (MAIN), trenches, the overall war (covered by the separate topic world-war-i)
The Great Depression (named as later context, not covered)
The Progressive Era (named as background, treated in its own topic)

claims.claim: When war broke out in Europe in 1914, the United States declared neutrality and President Woodrow Wilson urged Americans to be neutral in thought as well as action, but American trade and bank loans flowed increasingly to the Allies, binding the U.S. economy to Britain and France.

A German U-boat sank the British liner RMS Lusitania on 7 May 1915, killing nearly 1,200 people including 128 Americans; after a pledge to restrain submarine attacks, Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare in early 1917, sinking American shipping.

In January 1917 German Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann sent a coded telegram to the German minister in Mexico proposing a German-Mexican alliance and offering Mexico the return of lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona; British intelligence intercepted and decoded it, presented it to the U.S. on 24 February 1917, and it was published on 1 March 1917, inflaming American opinion. Congress declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917.

The Selective Service Act, signed 18 May 1917, established a national draft; about 24 million men ultimately registered and the army expanded rapidly. Wartime agencies including the War Industries Board (Bernard Baruch) and the Food Administration (Herbert Hoover) directed the economy, and the government financed the war largely through Liberty Bonds.

The Committee on Public Information under George Creel ran a mass propaganda campaign, while the Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918 criminalized anti-war speech; roughly 2,000 people were prosecuted, and Socialist leader Eugene V. Debs was sentenced to ten years for an anti-war, anti-draft speech.

Wartime labor demand and the desire to escape Jim Crow drew hundreds of thousands of Black Americans from the rural South to Northern industrial cities in what became known as the Great Migration; over a million women also entered the workforce, and the Nineteenth Amendment granting women the vote was ratified in 1920.

The American Expeditionary Forces under General John J. Pershing entered heavy combat in 1918 (Belleau Wood in June, the Second Battle of the Marne in July, and the Meuse-Argonne Offensive from September to November), helping tip the balance toward Allied victory; about 116,000 American servicemembers died — roughly half in combat and half from disease, especially the 1918 influenza — and around 200,000 were wounded before the armistice of 11 November 1918.

In his Fourteen Points speech to Congress on 8 January 1918, Wilson called for open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, self-determination, and — as his centerpiece — a League of Nations. He secured the League Covenant in the Treaty of Versailles (signed 28 June 1919) but compromised on most other points.

The U.S. Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles on 19 November 1919 and again on 19 March 1920. Republican leader Henry Cabot Lodge and the reservationists objected especially to Article X of the League Covenant (a collective-security obligation), and Wilson refused to compromise; the United States never joined the League and turned toward isolationism.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact number of men drafted versus total who served
positions: The OpenStax paraphrase gives roughly five million drafted plus volunteers; the standard Selective Service record is about 24 million registered with roughly 2.8 million inducted and about 4.7 million serving in all forces.
Figures vary by whether one counts registrations, inductions, volunteers, or total force size.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the well-established registration figure (~24 million) and describes the draft's scale qualitatively rather than asserting a contested exact induction count.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The size of the WWI-era Great Migration
positions: OpenStax cites roughly 350,000 Black Americans moving to Northern cities between 1910 and 1920; other estimates put the wartime wave (1916-1919) closer to half a million.
The larger Great Migration (about six million) spans 1916-1970 and is far broader than the WWI period.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the wartime movement as 'hundreds of thousands' as the first wave of the Great Migration, avoiding a single contested figure.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft in lessons.json was machine-generated boilerplate ('...is a foundational concept in History...') with no substantive factual claims to verify.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate entirely with verified, sourced content.

Presented draftee counts and Great Migration figures as ranges/qualitative rather than as the single contested numbers that appear in some summaries.
